1964 Studebaker Wagonaire Junkyard Find Is a Rare Classic With an Innovative Feature
12 photos
Photo: Steve Magnante/YouTube
In 1961, Studebaker hired industrial designer Brooks Stevens to restyle the Hawk series and the Lark on a limited budget. He was also tasked with expanding the company's limited model range, which resulted in the Wagonaire hitting showrooms for the 1963 model year.
The Wagonaire was based on the Lark compact, which was already available as a station wagon. However, the Wagoinare was brand-new above the beltline, with the roofline inspired by Stevens' 1959 Scimitar concept. More importantly, it had a retractable panel over the cargo bay, a feature that wasn't available on any other wagon at the time.
Brooks developed the partially retractable roof in 1962 on a prototype called Skyview. But with Studebaker unable to develop a brand-new car, Stevens opted to redesign it for the Lark-based Wagonaire. The panel retracted into the forward section of the roof, where it locked into position. The headliner was lowered to provide clearance for the roof panel and the tracks.
The sliding roof enabled the Wagonaire to haul items that were too tall to fit inside a regular wagon trunk. Studebaker bragged that it could transport standard-size refrigerators in an upright position but also advertised the vehicle as an open-air convertible.
Print ads include photos of people stargazing through a telescope from the open rear bay or children playing with balloons while sitting in the trunk. But the Wagonaire didn't catch on as a leisure vehicle. And needless to say, the ability to haul tall items didn't make it particularly popular either.
Built from 1963 until 1966, the Wagonaire moved just under 20,000 units. Nearly 12,000 of these cars were sold in the first year, with an additional 5,163 delivered in 1964. About 12,000 are said to have been sold with the sliding roof feature (Studebaker also offered a regular roof version in all years except 1965).
Unfortunately, most of these grocery-getters are no longer around. While some have been restored and are still on the road, most are rotting away in junkyards and barns. Classic car enthusiasts recently found a 1964 example in a junkyard in Halifax, Massachusetts. It's one of those vehicles that was built before Studebaker closed its South Bend plant, and, yes, it has the sliding roof.
Studebaker sold 5,163 units during the 1964 model year. That number isn't small enough to call this wagon rare, but the original engine that's still under the hood suggests that it's actually pretty scarce. The mill in question is an inline-six. Studebaker offered both straight-six and V8 powerplants that year, and the former found its way into only a third of all the cars.
The mill is a 194-cubic-inch (3.2-liter) six-cylinder and was favored by 1,784 customers. This Wagonaire is most likely a base Commander model, which means it's one of 1,206 units made, according to existing data. The Challenger version would be much rarer, with only 453 units made.
The sliding roof panel is still in place, which is pretty cool, but the Studebaker is in a sorry state. It's quite obvious that it's been sitting for decades, and it has developed severe rust issues. Is it worth rescuing? Well, let's say that it wouldn't make sense financially since these wagons are far from valuable today.
However, with most of these cars having already morphed into rust buckets, examples that are still in one piece should be rescued in order to keep the Wagonaire legacy alive. Hopefully, someone will want to make it their labor of love, and we'll see it back on the road someday.
